heading: Hierarchy & Applied Analysis
outline: Empson on 'Pastoral' Identification (pp. 123-127): cross-class courtship in literary genre; comic primness; irony as social strategy
The 'Invidious' as Imitation in Veblen (pp. 127-132): competition as out-imitation; consubstantiality by community of ways; money as symbolic/dialectical abstraction
Priority of the 'Idea' (pp. 132-137): three orders of cultural identification (accidental/analogical/generative); occupational psychosis; symbolic motive prior to economic
A Metaphorical View of Hierarchy (pp. 137-142): the sea-myth; reversibility of rank at level of principle; entelechial tendency; hierarchic psychosis; scapegoat as faction-ritual
Diderot on 'Pantomime' (pp. 142-145): hierarchic disorder in Neveu de Rameau; pantomime as universal choreography of position; Lui as convergence of royal disorder
Generic, Specific, and Individual Motives in Rochefoucauld (pp. 145-150): courtly morality; six-moment analysis of self-love; prince/principle pun; God as ultimate division
De Gourmont on 'Dissociation' (pp. 149-154): breaking automatic identifications; god-incarnate pattern in every commonplace; realistic vs. imagistic analysis of abstractions
Pascal on 'Directing the Intention' (pp. 154-158): Pauline element in language; casuistry as abstraction-embodiment; Jesuit directed intention as rhetorical device

Administrative Rhetoric in Machiavelli (pp. 158-167): scene-act and agent-act ratios; nonverbal conditions as symbolic persuasion; ruler/ruled identification; conspiracy as the fact, universality as the fiction
Dante's De Vulgari Eloquentia (pp. 167-170): hierarchic language criteria; noble vernacular as pre-grammatical speech; infancy and the unconscious; Lawrence parallel
Rhetoric in the Middle Ages / McKeon survey (pp. 170-174): administrative rhetoric extending into medicine; nonverbal apparatus as symbolic persuasion
Infancy, Mystery, and Persuasion (pp. 174-180): ten-step synthesis from persuasion to theology; mystery as intrinsic to courtship-communication; two kinds of mystification

concepts.label: Hierarchy
concepts.gloss: Universal motivational-symbolic principle organizing existence on a scale of higher/lower; inevitable in systematic thought and growth; reversible at the level of pure principle; generator of courtship, mystery, and mystification.

concepts.label: Hierarchic psychosis
concepts.gloss: The pervasive motivational disposition toward rank-consciousness, ascent, and social position produced when the hierarchic principle structures consciousness; manifests as courtship, comic primness, and pantomime.

concepts.label: Entelechial principle
concepts.gloss: The tendency to treat the culminating or highest stage of any hierarchy as the representative 'image' of the entire 'idea'; makes the prince representative of order, thereby mystifying particular privilege as universal principle.

concepts.label: Identification
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical-symbolic mechanism behind imitation, emulation, and competitive conformity; achieved through community of ways (consubstantiality); Empson's pastoral = cross-class identification by rhetorical indirection.

concepts.label: Consubstantiality
concepts.gloss: Shared symbolic substance achieved through imitation of underlying principles rather than surface insignia; community of ways is the mechanism of consubstantiation across divided social positions.

concepts.label: Imitation
concepts.gloss: The master dramatistic concept subsuming competition, emulation, and the invidious; makes for consubstantiality by community of ways; competition = out-imitation; symbolic motive more general than the pecuniary.

concepts.label: Mystery
concepts.gloss: Not only ideological mystification of class but an intrinsic property of communication between different kinds of beings; emerges from the courtship structure of all persuasion; the 'mystery' of hierarchy is the mystery of persuasion itself.

concepts.label: Courtship
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical modality of communication across social difference; present whenever hierarchy structures relations between classes; ranges from outright flattery to ironically veiled challenge; the abstract paradigm of all persuasion.

concepts.label: Administrative rhetoric
concepts.gloss: Rhetoric that includes nonverbal, material operations — spectacles, military force, institutional apparatus — as well as verbal address; nonverbal conditions persuade by their 'meaning' (symbolic character), not merely material effect.

concepts.label: The invidious (Veblen, critically assessed)
concepts.gloss: Veblen's term for comparison-of-persons-in-respect-of-worth; Burke argues it is a partisan special case of the more general concept of imitation, masquerading as scientific neutrality.

concepts.label: Occupational psychosis (Dewey)
concepts.gloss: Imaginative transference of principles from one professional domain to a general worldview; Shaw constructs a philosophy of creative evolution on the analogy of his craft as playwright.

concepts.label: Pantomime (Diderot)
concepts.gloss: The choreography of social position — postures, obsequiousness, ritual deference — that enacts hierarchic arrangement; Burke's term for the hierarchic psychosis made visible in bodily performance.

concepts.label: Comic primness (Empson)
concepts.gloss: Ironic-apologetic attitude of a privileged person who questions but ultimately resigns to the conditions of privilege; paradigmatic of the embarrassments that mystified class produces; a suspended act between deference and challenge.

concepts.label: Directing the intention (Pascal/Jesuit)
concepts.gloss: Rhetorical device of re-attributing a performed act to a socially approved purpose; exploits the gap between act and symbolic framing; generalized by Burke to all administrative rhetoric.

concepts.label: Infancy
concepts.gloss: The pre-verbal, sub-verbal, and unconscious strata of meaning that give symbols their resonance beyond explicit content; Dante's valorization of the vernacular points toward identification with the unconscious as a rhetorical resource.

concepts.label: Priority of the 'Idea'
concepts.gloss: The claim that the laws of symbols are prior to any particular economic or property structure; the 'idea' (generating principle) transcends its material instantiations and is more generative than economic determinism alone.

concepts.label: Dissociation (De Gourmont)
concepts.gloss: Intellectual practice of severing automatic associations between facts and abstract ideals; clarifies how identification operates; limited by over-reliance on image vs. act/verb; valuable as a cleansing transition to rationally adopted new associations.

concepts.label: Scene-act ratio (Grammar cross-reference)
concepts.gloss: Pentad ratio: act proper to a given scene/situation; deployed by Burke to analyze Machiavelli's first 24 chapters; scenic conditions determine the rhetorically appropriate act.

concepts.label: Agent-act ratio (Grammar cross-reference)
concepts.gloss: Pentad ratio: act proper to a given agent's nature/temperament; deployed by Burke to analyze Machiavelli's penultimate chapter; character determines action independently of scenic conditions.

concepts.label: Pure persuasion (terminus of ten-step synthesis)
concepts.gloss: The terminal limit of the persuasive principle when abstract courtship is taken to its ultimate form: communication between the most divided kinds of being, culminating in theology and the address to God.

concepts.label: Terministic screen (implicit)
concepts.gloss: Veblen's choice of 'invidious' as his master term screens out the more general principle of imitation and consubstantiality; choice of terminology constitutes and constrains the analysis it enables.

concepts.label: Scapegoat
concepts.gloss: Ritual use of another class/group as a vessel for dyslogistic vocabulary; enables hierarchic factions to externalize shared vices; the katharma that makes hierarchic division ritually gratifying.

positions.claim: The hierarchic principle is inevitable in systematic thought; no particular hierarchy is inevitable, but the principle itself is indigenous to all well-rounded human thinking.

Competition is better described as men's attempt to out-imitate one another; 'invidious' is a special case of imitation, which is in turn a special case of consubstantiality-through-community-of-ways.
The 'pecuniary' motive should be analyzed as a special case of the linguistic/symbolic motive; the laws of symbols are prior to any particular property structure.

Machiavelli's Prince is best understood as a manual of administrative rhetoric in which nonverbal operations (military, spectacle, institutional) persuade by their symbolic meaning, not merely material force.

Mystery is intrinsic to the persuasive act as such, not merely an ideological mystification of class; the courtship structure of communication-between-kinds generates mystery as an a priori condition of identification.

The entelechial tendency — treating the culminating stage as the representative image of the whole — makes hierarchy mystifying by confounding the universal principle with the particular privilege of the top rank.

Self-love (La Rochefoucauld) is a social term for individual divisiveness; the courtly-social motive is prior to the individualistic one; the individual is defined by his place in a hierarchic institution.

calleja_pim_candidates.rationale: Hierarchy as rank/prestige structure; out-imitation competition; entelechial pull toward top-ranked player/guild; leaderboards and gear-score as hierarchic psychosis operationalized in game design.
Community of in-game ways (pathing, build strategies, tactical imitation) as consubstantiality through shared practice; game space as hierarchically organized scene generating appropriate acts.
Quest-framing as 'directing the intention': narrative layer re-attributes acts (kill/collect/explore) to socially approved purposes (heroism, sacrifice, civic duty), producing identification.

Mystery/infancy as subliminal affective resonance exceeding explicit content; atmospheric and sound-design rhetoric as designed phenomenology of the pre-verbal; Attitude as incipient act operationalized in designed game experience.

tensions.description: Veblen's reductive 'invidious' motive vs. Burke's claim that imitation/consubstantiality is the more fundamental term; Veblen reveals a superficial rhetoric while leaving a profounder rhetoric unanalyzed.

Ideological priority of the economic (Marx) vs. symbolic/linguistic priority (Burke); Burke attempts a functional division: the economic limits the ideological but the symbolic is more general and prior.
Hierarchy as natural/inevitable principle vs. particular hierarchies as contingent and crumbling; the universality of the principle is distinct from the legitimacy of any given arrangement.
Mystery as ideological mystification (Marx/Carlyle) vs. mystery as intrinsic to the persuasive act itself; the second kind of mystification cannot be cleared away by mere debunking.

Machiavelli as founder of political 'science' (Cassirer) vs. Burke's reading of The Prince as administrative rhetoric; naturalism vs. supernaturalism is a false antithesis that prevents analysis of the book's rhetorical form.

De Gourmont's imagistic archetypation (ideas as worn-out images) vs. Burke's realistic treatment of abstractions as verbs/acts; De Gourmont's analysis corrects idealism but undersells the verbal/dramatistic dimension.
